title: Starved for Wisdom in the Age of Information
author: J. Chase Davis
summary: A sermon preached at The Well Church in Boulder on July 12, 2026, drawing on three passages from Proverbs to address the paradox of information-abundant but wisdom-starved modern life. Davis argues that as responsibilities increase, the need for wise counsel grows rather than shrinks, and that Christ is the ultimate counselor—not merely a comforter but a guide who provides wisdom for real decisions. On plans: the plans of the heart belong to man, but their outcome belongs to God; the error is either having no plans (masked immaturity) or assuming they'll unfold as designed. On trust: the beginning of wisdom is fearing the Lord, which means turning toward God, not merely away from evil. On pride: arrogance is assuming the Lord's place—visible not in self-examination but in how you treat people. Confidence, rightly understood, is steadiness in God and in the duties he has assigned, trusting the results to him.
points: Information has never been more available, yet people are paralyzed by decisions and starved for wisdom—and the growing number turning to AI for wisdom underscores the depth of the gap.
As responsibilities increase, the need for wise counsel grows, not shrinks: the stakes for a husband and father are higher than for a single man, requiring more counsel, not less.
Two errors in planning: having no plans (often mistaken for spiritual maturity, actually immaturity) and assuming plans will unfold as designed (failing to trust providence).
Pride is most clearly visible in how you treat people, not in how carefully you examine your own thoughts; some of the most introspective people Davis has met were the most prideful.
True confidence is steadiness in the Lord and in your assigned duties, knowing what you're good at and trusting the results to God—not the self-deprecation that is pride wearing a costume.
quotes: we live in a day where information has never been more readily available and yet people are starved for wisdom. Paralyzed by decisions. Overwhelmed and anxious.
As your responsibilities and opportunities increase, you need more of it not less. You need more wise counsel as a husband and father than you did when you were a single man.

Arrogance is assuming the place of the Lord. It is his rule, his power, his authority to see the heart and establish paths. Arrogance is assuming a level of control and authority that is not afforded to you.
Some of the most prideful people I’ve met have been the most introspective. Instead, you will see pride more clearly in how you treat people than in how you audit your own thoughts.
You don’t think of yourself too highly, but you know what you’re good at, and you trust the results to God. That’s confidence.
